title: Draupadi
hook: hungry sages are bathing at the river, the vessel is empty because Draupadi has eaten, and Krishna arrives asking for food

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi at home: asked for a charm, she gave a list of chores and remembered keeping the accounts at Indraprastha. Did you name someone's unseen work? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

Dinner is over. The plates are washed. The cook has finally sat down and eaten her own meal. And then there's a knock. A great sage is at the door, with a crowd of disciples behind him, and they would like to be fed. They're going down to the river to bathe first. They'll be back soon. Hungry. In the forest years of the Mahabharata, this is Draupadi's evening, and the sage is Durvasa, a man the stories remember for his temper and his curses. Today: an empty pot, and the guest who scraped it.
screen: `THE MEAL IS OVER.` → `A SAGE AT THE DOOR, WITH DISCIPLES.` → `AN EMPTY POT.`

segments.voice: First, the pot. Early in the exile, the epic says, the sun gives Yudhishthira a vessel that will feed the household and its guests, every day, until Draupadi has eaten. So Draupadi serves everyone first, and eats last, and then the vessel is done for the day. That rule is the whole problem. Some tellings of the epic carry the next part. Duryodhana, hoping to trap his cousins, sends Durvasa to visit at exactly the wrong hour, after Draupadi has eaten. The sage and his disciples go off to bathe. Draupadi has nothing to give them, and a sage refused hospitality might curse the house. So she turns to Krishna, in her mind. And Krishna arrives. His first words, here in paraphrase, are: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat. Draupadi is almost in despair. The pot is empty, she tells him. That's why I called you. He asks to see it anyway. Stuck to the rim is one small bit of leaf, a scrap of vegetable. Krishna eats it, and says, may this satisfy the one who is the soul of the world. Down at the river, the sages suddenly feel full, as if they'd eaten a feast. Embarrassed to come back and refuse a meal, they slip away. Three things sit inside this little story. It's funny: the rescuer shows up asking to be fed. It's tender: Krishna takes the leftover, the scrap no one would serve a guest. And it puts Draupadi at the center of the household. The food lasts until she eats. Everyone's meal is measured by her patience.
screen: `A VESSEL THAT FEEDS UNTIL SHE EATS` · `A SAGE ARRIVES AFTER THE MEAL` · `KRISHNA COMES ASKING FOR FOOD` · `ONE LEAF ON THE RIM`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the last bit on the rim. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a time you had almost nothing left to give: no time, no energy, no patience. Don't argue with it. Just see the empty pot. Then look again, slowly, for one small thing still on the rim. A kind word. Five minutes. A glass of water. With each breath out, let that small thing be enough for now. If you pray, you can offer it, the way Draupadi turned to Krishna. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi. She served everyone first, and when the pot was empty and guests were coming, Krishna made a meal of one leaf on the rim. Today's word.
Your line: Draupadi. Today, when you think you have nothing left for someone, look once more for the leaf on the rim, and give that. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Hindus hear the story of Durvasa's visit in retellings of the Mahabharata and in devotional storytelling, where the vessel of plenty and Krishna eating the last leaf are told as signs of his care for those who call on him.

turn to Krishna in your mind.

original.note: Sanskrit, a name later tradition gives the sun's vessel: akshaya, unfailing, and patra, vessel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic pot of endless food.
what it means: the pot feeds everyone only until Draupadi eats, so the one who serves eats last.
what a scholar hears: Krishna eats one leaf from the rim and calls on the soul of the world to be satisfied, and guests far away are fed.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parvan), Yudhishthira receives a vessel from Surya (Critical Edition 3.3; Ganguli section 3)

notes: The Durvasa episode is found in the vulgate Vana Parva (Ganguli 261–263) but, as far as the writer knows, is not in the body of the Critical Edition; the voice says 'some tellings of the epic carry the next part'. Please confirm.

Confirm the details: Duryodhana sends Durvasa to arrive after Draupadi has eaten; Krishna says he is hungry; a particle of vegetable or leaf on the rim; Krishna's words about satisfying the soul of the universe; the sages feel full while bathing and leave.
The vessel's rule (it gives food until Draupadi has eaten) is from Vana Parva 3; year 3 day 777 told the gift of the vessel from Yudhishthira's side, so this day keeps that brief.
'akshaya patra' as the vessel's name is common in later retelling; the voice does not use it. Check the original-game note and Devanagari.
Editor pass: replaced the repeated 'Turn it a few ways' transition; 'the god takes the leftover' changed to 'Krishna takes the leftover' so the narrator does not assert belief.
